'''William W. Menasco''' is a [[topologist]] and a professor at the [[University at Buffalo]].  He is best known for his work in [[knot theory]].

==Biography==
Menasco received his [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] in 1975, and his [[Ph.D.]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1981, where his advisor was [[Robion Kirby]]. He served as assistant professor at [[Rutgers University]] from 1981 to 1984. He then taught as a visiting professor at the [[University at Buffalo]] where he became an assistant professor in 1985, an associate professor in 1991. In 1994 he became a professor at the [[University at Buffalo]] where he currently serves.<ref>[http://www.math.buffalo.edu/~menasco/menasco.html Homepage of William W. Menasco (continued)<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==Work==
Menasco proved that a [[link (knot theory)|link]] with an [[alternating diagram]], such as an [[alternating link]], will be non-[[split link|split]] if and only if the diagram is connected.

Menasco, along with [[Morwen Thistlethwaite]] proved the [[Tait conjectures|Tait flyping conjecture]], which states that, given any two reduced [[knot diagram|alternating diagrams]] <math>D1,D2</math> of an oriented, prime [[alternating link]], <math>D1</math> may be transformed to <math>D2</math> by means of a sequence of certain simple moves called [[flype]]s.<ref>{{MathWorld|TaitsKnotConjectures|Tait's Knot Conjectures}}</ref>
